title: APRA Finalises Capital Treatment of Longevity Products, Effective July 1, 2026: Insurers Can Use an 'Advanced Illiquidity Premium' With a 45% Floor and Extra Controls
summary: On March 31, 2026 APRA finalised amendments letting life insurers use an 'advanced illiquidity premium' to set capital for longevity products, with added governance, reporting and asset controls and a 45% floor kept after consultation; the changes took effect on July 1, 2026.
description:
Australia's prudential regulator has changed how life insurers must hold capital against products that pay income for life, in an effort to make such products easier to offer. The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) released a response paper on March 31, 2026, finalising amendments to the capital treatment of longevity products, according to a summary by the law firm Regulation Tomorrow. The changes took effect on July 1, 2026. They followed consultations in June 2025 and October 2025, and APRA published an attachment summarising changes from the October 2025 versions.

Longevity products are insurance products that guarantee income for as long as the policyholder lives, such as lifetime annuities. They expose the insurer to longevity risk, the risk that people live longer than expected, and the insurer must hold capital against it. Because the insurer's promises stretch over decades and are usually matched with long-term, relatively illiquid assets, the way capital rules treat the link between those assets and liabilities has large effects on the cost of the product.

The core change is optional. Insurers can choose to use what APRA calls an "advanced illiquidity premium" (AILP) to set their capital requirements for these products. An illiquidity premium is the extra return available from assets that cannot easily be sold, and the AILP lets an insurer recognise more of it when it values long-term liabilities backed by such assets. APRA paired the option with added controls on governance, reporting and the assets backing the portfolio. The regulator's aim is to allow capital requirements to reflect the long-term nature of the liabilities while retaining safeguards for policyholders.

Consultation feedback, according to the summary, was broadly positive. Some respondents asked for changes to the risk allowance floor and to how the AILP applies in the credit spread stress charge under the life insurance prudential standard LPS 114. Views on the restrictions on assets were mixed. APRA decided to keep the AILP settings, saying they "remain sound and strike the right balance" between capital efficiency and risk controls. It made wording changes: eligible products are called "longevity products" in the response paper and "illiquid liabilities" in the standards.

The most debated point was the 45% floor. APRA kept it. The regulator acknowledged that the floor limits the capital benefit when credit spreads are very narrow, as they are now, and that in those conditions the AILP may be equal to the Standard Illiquidity Premium, meaning the new option would offer no extra benefit. However, its historical analysis found that such conditions are rare, so the evidence did not justify lowering the floor. In plain terms, insurers hoping for large capital savings today may find that the benefit is smaller than they would like while credit spreads are tight, though the option may be worth more if spreads widen.

For implementation, APRA released a reporting template for insurers using the AILP and sought feedback on it by May 12, 2026. The July 1 start date meant insurers could begin using the option from the start of the new financial year, though the sources reviewed do not say how many insurers plan to do so.

The policy sits within a wider effort to improve retirement incomes. Australia's superannuation system has accumulated large balances, and as more members move into retirement the question of how to turn savings into reliable income becomes more pressing. APRA's stated direction, as summarised, is to let insurers invest in sustainable, competitively priced products that help Australians retire with confidence, although the response paper summary reviewed here does not quote a named APRA member on the point.

What should readers make of it? The change is permissive, not mandatory, and it reduces a technical barrier to product design and does not itself create demand. Whether insurers launch more lifetime income products depends on pricing, investment opportunities, distribution through super funds and consumer interest. The 45% floor means the capital relief will not be as large as some insurers wanted, and the added asset controls mean that those who use the option must meet governance and reporting standards.

There are also questions about risk. A more generous recognition of illiquidity can reduce capital held against long-term liabilities, and APRA has chosen to pair it with restrictions to prevent insurers from taking on excessive risk in search of yield. How those restrictions work in practice, and how strictly they are supervised, will determine whether the framework strengthens or weakens policyholder protection. The summary notes that views on the asset restrictions were mixed, which suggests the details will continue to be debated.

For consumers, the immediate effect is none: policies already in force are unaffected, and any new products will take time to appear. For the industry, the next steps are to decide whether to adopt the AILP, to prepare the required governance and reporting, and to watch how APRA applies the floor. The regulator's analysis implies that the answer will depend heavily on the credit-spread environment, which is outside insurers' control.
source_name: Regulation Tomorrow (summary of APRA's March 31, 2026 response paper) and APRA

key_points: APRA issued a response paper on March 31, 2026 finalising amendments to the capital treatment of longevity products, effective July 1, 2026, after consultations in June and October 2025.

Insurers may choose to use an 'advanced illiquidity premium' (AILP) to set their capital requirements for these products, paired with added controls on governance, reporting and the assets backing the portfolio.
APRA kept the AILP settings, saying they 'remain sound and strike the right balance' between capital efficiency and risk controls, and retained a 45% floor.
APRA acknowledged that the floor limits the capital benefit when credit spreads are very narrow, but its historical analysis found such conditions are rare.
Eligible products are called 'longevity products' in the response paper and 'illiquid liabilities' in the standards, and APRA released a reporting template for insurers using the AILP.
why_it_matters: Australians are retiring with large superannuation balances and need ways to turn savings into lifetime income. Lower or more stable capital requirements could make it cheaper for insurers to offer guaranteed lifetime income products, while APRA's controls aim to keep those promises safe.

title: MAS Names 42 Finalists for the 2026 Global FinTech Hackcelerator and Awards, With Zurich Insurance Challenging Startups to Help SMEs Quantify Business Risk
summary: The Monetary Authority of Singapore announced 42 finalists on October 19, 2026 for the Global FinTech Hackcelerator and SFF FinTech Excellence Awards, including 18 solutions to challenges from GXS Bank, Julius Baer and Zurich Insurance, with demo day on November 18 and winners revealed on November 19.
description:
Singapore's financial regulator has moved its annual fintech competition from the application stage to the finals, and the shortlist shows what banks and insurers want from startups. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) announced on October 19, 2026 that 42 finalists had been chosen for the 2026 Global FinTech Hackcelerator and the SFF FinTech Excellence Awards. MAS had invited applications for both programmes in June 2026, with an earlier outline describing a focus on artificial intelligence in banking, wealth management and risk assessment for small businesses. The finalist announcement confirms those themes and sets the dates for the final stage.

The Global FinTech Hackcelerator is organised by MAS together with the Global Finance and Technology Network (GFTN), a not-for-profit entity set up by MAS. It works by asking established companies, called corporate champions, to set a problem and inviting fintech firms around the world to propose market-ready solutions. This year's three champions and challenges are GXS Bank, a digital bank, which asked for integration of credit and fraud risk modelling in digital banking; Julius Baer, a global wealth manager, which asked how to reimagine wealth management for a digitally native generation; and Zurich Insurance, which asked for help enabling small and medium-sized enterprises to better assess, quantify and proactively manage their business risk exposure. Eighteen finalists were shortlisted. The release names the categories but, in the version reviewed, does not list the finalists themselves, which are in annexes to the announcement.

Prizes and follow-on support are specified. There is one winner per problem statement, three in total, and each receives S$80,000. Finalists can explore pilot engagements with their corporate champion, and can apply for the Global FinTech Hackcelerator Scale-Up Grant under the Financial Sector Technology and Innovation scheme, known as FSTI 4.0. The grant provides follow-on funding for product development, commercial milestones and establishing a presence in Singapore. The finalists present their solutions at a Demo Day on November 18, 2026, held as part of the Singapore FinTech Festival (SFF), which runs from November 18 to 20.

The second programme, the SFF FinTech Excellence Awards, is organised by MAS and the Singapore FinTech Association (SFA), supported by PwC Singapore. It recognises corporates and individuals whose initiatives have significantly contributed to the fintech ecosystem and advanced innovation in financial services. The awards received 131 submissions across six categories. In the five corporate categories there were 119 submissions, and four finalists were shortlisted in each, for 20 in total. The categories are Emerging FinTech, Financial Inclusivity, Regulatory Leader, Sustainable Innovator and a thematic award for AI Champion, and each has one winner receiving S$50,000. The individual category, the FinTech Mentor Award, received 13 submissions and four finalists, of whom three will win S$5,000 each. Adding up the 18 Hackcelerator finalists, 20 corporate finalists and four mentor finalists gives the total of 42 in the announcement. Winners will be revealed at the awards dinner on November 19, 2026.

Eleven organisations contributed to the FinTech Gives Back initiative this year, which supports promising fintech innovators: Finmo, Ripple, HeyMax, Aspire, dtcpay, Experian, LexisNexis, Sfye, Sumsub, Width and YouTrip. Kenneth Gay, MAS's chief fintech officer, said the Hackcelerator and Awards aim to help promising fintech solutions gain industry traction and scale into regional and global markets. SFA president Holly Fang noted that 2026 marks the association's tenth year, and Wong Wanyi of PwC Singapore said the awards are entering a new chapter after their tenth anniversary.

The announcement sits within a wider set of MAS initiatives that the release lists. On July 3, 2026, MAS and industry published a white paper called Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime, or SAFR, on safeguards for AI agents in finance, developed under the BuildFin.ai initiative. On August 26, SFF 2026 was announced with a theme of exploring five forces reshaping global finance. And on August 31, MAS committed S$220 million over three years under the renewed FSTI 4.0 scheme. Together they show a regulator that backs both the technology and the rules around it.

For the insurance sector, the Zurich challenge is the most relevant element. Small and medium-sized businesses often struggle to understand what risks they face and how much cover they need, and insurers struggle to assess those risks cheaply. A solution that helps an owner of a small firm quantify exposures could, in principle, lead to better-targeted cover and lower distribution costs, though the announcement does not describe any specific product and no results can be expected until after the demo day. What readers can verify is the structure: a regulator-backed contest, three corporate problems, S$80,000 for each winner and a route to pilots and grants.

What to watch next is the Demo Day on November 18 and the awards dinner on November 19, where the winners will be named. After that, the useful signs will be whether winners secure pilots with their corporate champions and whether any move to set up in Singapore through the scale-up grant. The competition does not guarantee commercial results, but it shows what problems major financial firms are willing to put in front of startups.
source_name: Monetary Authority of Singapore (October 19, 2026) and MAS media release inviting applications (June 2026)
image_alt: Digital network graphic representing financial technology innovation (illustrative)
key_points: MAS named 42 finalists: 18 for the Global FinTech Hackcelerator, 20 across five corporate awards and four for the FinTech Mentor Award.

The Hackcelerator challenges come from GXS Bank on integrating credit and fraud risk modelling, Julius Baer on wealth management for a digitally native generation, and Zurich Insurance on helping SMEs assess, quantify and manage business risk.

There is one winner per challenge, each receiving S$80,000, and finalists can seek pilots with the corporate champion and apply for a Global FinTech Hackcelerator Scale-Up Grant under the FSTI 4.0 scheme.
The awards drew 131 submissions, with five corporate categories paying S$50,000 per winner and three Mentor Award winners receiving S$5,000 each.

Demo Day is November 18, 2026, the awards dinner is November 19 and the Singapore FinTech Festival runs November 18 to 20, while MAS committed S$220 million over three years under FSTI 4.0 on August 31.
why_it_matters: Singapore's regulator uses these programmes to steer fintech effort toward problems that banks and insurers say they have. The insurance challenge, helping small businesses measure their risk, shows where regulators and insurers think technology could close the protection gap for smaller firms.

title: Buy Now, Pay Later Became FCA-Regulated on July 15, 2026: Affordability Checks, Ombudsman Access and Section 75 Refund Rights for Interest-Free Instalment Credit
summary: From July 15, 2026, UK interest-free 'Deferred Payment Credit' offered by a lender separate from the retailer is regulated by the FCA under policy statement PS26/1: lenders must check affordability, give key information, and customers can use the Financial Ombudsman and, in some cases, Section 75 refund rights.
description:
Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL), the interest-free instalment option that appears at online and in-store checkouts, has been brought inside the UK's financial regulation. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) calls the product Deferred Payment Credit, or DPC, and the new regime began on July 15, 2026. The FCA published its final rules on February 11, 2026, in policy statement PS26/1, after legislation was published in July 2025. According to analysis by the law firm A&O Shearman, the FCA made only minor amendments to its draft rules and guidance, which were set out in consultation paper CP25/23.

The scale of the market explains the interest. A&O Shearman's summary says the BNPL market grew from £0.06 billion in 2017 to over £13 billion in 2024. For years it sat largely outside consumer credit regulation, partly because interest-free, short-term credit was exempt.

What is covered? The FCA's consumer page explains that the regulated product is interest-free credit repayable in 12 or fewer instalments over 12 months or less. It is regulated when the lender and the supplier of the goods or services are different businesses, as is typical when a shopper uses a third-party BNPL provider at a retailer's checkout. Credit offered by the same business that is selling the goods is not regulated under this regime. Importantly, agreements taken out before July 15, 2026 remain unregulated, so the new protections do not apply retrospectively.

What must lenders do? According to the FCA, lenders must hold FCA authorisation or be registered under the temporary permissions regime to offer DPC. They must check that the customer can afford to repay before the agreement starts. A&O Shearman notes that lenders must assess creditworthiness for each DPC transaction, including those under £50, and that the FCA did not change the existing rules in its consumer credit sourcebook on this point. Lenders must give key information beforehand, including the amount to be borrowed, repayment dates and amounts, the late fee and the customer's rights and protections. If a customer misses a repayment, the lender must make contact and explain what it means, and must support customers who are struggling to repay.

The final rules softened some requirements. A&O Shearman reports that the amount of information in the key product information document was reduced: details on withdrawal, cancellation, early repayment, complaint rights to the Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS) and continuous payment authority move to "additional product information", although the key information must point customers to it. Lenders must tell customers whether they will, or may, check a credit reference agency before deciding on an agreement. Communications about missed payments need to explain the consequences arising from that missed payment, rather than every possible future consequence. Before terminating an agreement or taking enforcement action, firms must signpost free, impartial debt advice. Lenders no longer have to notify guarantors of missed payments. Unauthorised DPC lenders had to comply with the Consumer Duty by July 15, 2026.

One point that differs from the consultation concerns the Financial Ombudsman Service. A&O Shearman reports that the FOS voluntary jurisdiction does not cover DPC, contrary to what the consultation proposed, and that it excludes complaints before regulation began and activity from establishments in the EEA or Gibraltar. For consumers, the FCA's page says that if something goes wrong, they should complain to the lender first and, if unhappy with the response, can escalate to the Financial Ombudsman Service. The FCA also says people may be able to get a refund from the lender under Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act, the same protection they would have when paying by credit card, subject to the conditions of that law.

The transition arrangements prevent a sudden gap in the market. Firms that were carrying on DPC as of July 15, 2025 without the necessary permissions could register for the temporary permissions regime during a notification window that ran from May 15 to July 1, 2026. Those firms then have six months after July 15, 2026 to apply for full authorisation. The FCA's page tells consumers to check lenders using the FCA Firm Checker, selecting "Borrowing money, including credit card lending and credit information", and says the temporary permissions list includes 15 lenders, such as Clearpay and PayItMonthly. The six-month window means those firms must apply for full authorisation by about mid-January 2027.

Consumers get a few practical benefits. They should see clearer information before they sign up, an affordability assessment that may sometimes lead to a refusal, and contact and support if they fall behind. For those in financial difficulty, the FCA directs people to MoneyHelper's Debt Advice Locator to find free local services.

Two limits are worth remembering. First, the regime covers interest-free credit from a separate lender; other types of credit, such as credit cards or loans, are already regulated through other rules. Second, because earlier agreements are outside the regime, someone who took out BNPL in June may not have the same rights as someone who took it out in August.

For retailers, the change matters indirectly. Some BNPL providers may tighten approvals as they implement affordability checks, which could affect conversion rates at checkout, though the sources reviewed do not quantify any such effect. For the market as a whole, the move from light-touch to full regulation is a significant step, and the FCA's decision to run a temporary regime shows it wants products to remain available while standards rise.
source_name: Financial Conduct Authority (consumer BNPL page) and A&O Shearman (analysis of policy statement PS26/1)
image_alt: Online checkout representing Buy Now Pay Later credit (illustrative)
key_points: UK Buy Now, Pay Later, which the FCA calls Deferred Payment Credit (DPC), became regulated on July 15, 2026 under final rules published as PS26/1 on February 11, 2026.

Regulated DPC is interest-free, repayable in 12 or fewer instalments over 12 months or less, and offered by a lender that is a different business from the supplier of the goods; agreements taken out before July 15 stay unregulated.

Lenders must be FCA-authorised or in the temporary permissions regime, check that borrowers can afford repayments (including on transactions under £50), give key product information, contact customers who miss payments and support those in difficulty.
Customers can complain to the lender and then the Financial Ombudsman Service, and may be able to claim a refund from the lender under Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act.

The FCA lists 15 firms in the temporary permissions regime, including Clearpay and PayItMonthly, and those firms have six months after July 15 to apply for full authorisation; the market grew from £0.06 billion in 2017 to over £13 billion in 2024.
why_it_matters: Millions of UK shoppers use buy now, pay later at checkout, often without thinking of it as borrowing. Regulation means these lenders now face affordability checks and customer-protection rules, and users gain routes for complaints and refunds, though agreements made before July 15 are not covered.
